When the Omni was discovered by a probe on its way to Venus, it marked a beginning and an end. For two scant years, mankind questioned whether Russell's teapot was actually a real thing, or if it was just space debris, but that question was answered after the European Space Agency built a special probe to retrieve and safely bring it back.

At first it was named Russell's teapot, if only because it was shaped exactly like a teapot and it was found orbiting in space. Its name was changed almost immediately upon arriving at Earth, because it became clear that it was not a teapot; it was a tool of God, if not God himself. Anything poured into the teapot could be poured out as anything. Water could become wine, salt could become pepper, and lead could become gold. It was even possible to pour in a solid matter and have it pour out abstractions that could be felt by all in the room. In one notable case that spread across the internet, a gram of potassium sulfate was turned into love.

It became clear that the Omni was a representation of a question mankind had wondered -- can everything be explained? It was a physical manifestation of the theory of everything, just bizarrely in the form of a teapot. Its mechanism came to be called the perpendicular complex, which stated that in 11 dimensions of perpendicularity, that everything is connected to everything else. Just as black and white fall opposite on a single line, you can draw perpendicular opposites to them. Opaque opposite black, transparent opposite white, and translucent opposite gray. From there you can draw more perpendicular lines, until everything is connected to another in a chaotic web of all possibility.

In a way, it changed how we looked at the world. If black and white were considered opposites, but they fell on a line, what happened if we applied them to a square, a cube, a tesseract? The distance between the farthest corners just keeps growing. In the end, everything can be an opposite of something else, but in our mind we always assumed opposite was the shortest path and not the longest one.

Once we understood the Omni, the possibilities became endless. We could now control what came out, no matter what was put in. We could even put in nothing and still have it pour out whatever we wanted. We poured out the equation that drove the Omni, we poured out the Omni itself. We even poured out an entire universe and set it on the table so we could marvel as it evolved.

The world is different now, and it has only been ten years since we brought the Omni to the Earth. Science is no longer a quest for discovery, but instead an exercise in philosophy which is fed into the Omni, whereupon it pours the answers out to us. Anything we could want, we can get. Traditional science has died, replaced by the Omni. Economics has died, replaced by the Omni. Philosophy and mathematics remain, for they are the only fields that can understand the Omni, and program it. Soon the construction of the first wave of warp ships will be completed; each one powered by their own Omni.

How sad it is that our quest for knowledge has ended. It feels like cheating now, and as rightfully it should. What we have discovered is an abomination.

Mindfulness 'as good as anti-depressants for tackling depression'

I hate articles like this actually, but felt it worth sharing and commenting on.

The title, subtitle, and the beginning of the article strongly gives the impression that mindfulness and meditation is always as good as if not better than anti-depressants, which is absolutely not the case and is expanded on later in the article.

There is absolutely a place for non-pharmacological interventions and they should very often be tried first and utilized as much as possible as a first recourse Sometimes medication is the best route forward and should be used in conjunction with those non-pharmacological interventions, if only to stabilize the individual to the point where they can function and meaningfully engage in therapy and training in things like mindfulness and meditation.

Brain function and all that results from it is simply biochemistry, and drugs are a very important and often effective method if interacting with that biochemistry. We still have a tremendous amount to learn, probably way more than we currently know, but when applied appropriately what we know at this point can do wonders for people in some really rough places in their lives.

Based on what information I could find on the internet, there is actually very little difference between the efficacy of antidepressant medication and placebos, although strictly for the treatment of those without severe depression. http://www.nimh.nih.gov/about/director/2011/antidepressants-a-complicated-picture.shtml I think this article synthesizes it well, and seems credible.

In more severe forms of depression, antidepressants show greater efficacy. It is important to note that these clinical studies have primarily focused on reducing the symptoms of depression and not on a broader range of potential outcomes (such as changes in everyday functions, cognitive abilities, quality of life, etc.).

Mindfulness meditation stopped more people sliding back into depression than anti-depressants

to be misleading at best. Especially considering the large number of people more heavily influenced by headlines and the first paragraph or so of an article compared to the number of people who seriously read everything in depth and thoughtfully.
